Here \(a = \frac{1}{2}\) and \(r = \frac{1/4}{1/2} = \frac{1}{2}\).
Since \(|r| = \frac{1}{2} < 1\), the sum to infinity exists.
\(S = \frac{a}{1 - r} = \frac{1/2}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} = \frac{1/2}{1/2}\).
The sum to infinity exists and equals \(1\).

Here \(a = 2\) and \(r = \frac{4/3}{2} = \frac{2}{3}\).
Since \(|r| = \frac{2}{3} < 1\), the sum to infinity exists.
\(S = \frac{a}{1 - r} = \frac{2}{1 - \frac{2}{3}} = \frac{2}{\frac{1}{3}}\).
The sum to infinity exists and equals \(6\).

Here \(a = -3\) and \(r = \frac{1}{-3} = -\frac{1}{3}\).
Since \(|r| = \frac{1}{3} < 1\), the sum to infinity exists.
\(S = \frac{a}{1 - r} = \frac{-3}{1 - \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)} = \frac{-3}{\frac{4}{3}} = -3 \times \frac{3}{4}\).
The sum to infinity exists and equals \(-\frac{9}{4}\).

Here \(a = \frac{1}{5}\) and \(r = \frac{-2/5}{1/5} = -2\) (the same ratio holds throughout: \(\frac{4/5}{-2/5} = -2\)).
Since \(|r| = 2 > 1\), the terms do not tend to \(0\) and the geometric series diverges.
The sum to infinity does not exist.

Here \(a = 9\) and \(r = \frac{8.1}{9} = 0.9\) (check: \(\frac{7.29}{8.1} = 0.9\)).
Since \(|r| = 0.9 < 1\), the sum to infinity exists.
\(S = \frac{a}{1 - r} = \frac{9}{1 - 0.9} = \frac{9}{0.1}\).
The sum to infinity exists and equals \(90\).

Write the decimal as an infinite G.P.:
\(0.\overline{7} = 0.7 + 0.07 + 0.007 + \cdots\), with \(a = 0.7\) and \(r = 0.1\), and \(|r| < 1\).
\(S = \frac{a}{1 - r} = \frac{0.7}{1 - 0.1} = \frac{0.7}{0.9}\).
\(0.\overline{7} = \frac{7}{9}\).

Split off the integer part: \(2.\overline{4} = 2 + (0.4 + 0.04 + 0.004 + \cdots)\).
The bracket is an infinite G.P. with \(a = 0.4\), \(r = 0.1\), \(|r| < 1\), so its sum is \(\frac{0.4}{1 - 0.1} = \frac{4}{9}\).
\(2.\overline{4} = 2 + \frac{4}{9} = \frac{18 + 4}{9}\).
\(2.\overline{4} = \frac{22}{9}\).

Given \(r = \frac{2}{3}\) and \(S = \frac{a}{1 - r} = 12\).
\(\therefore a = S(1 - r) = 12\left(1 - \frac{2}{3}\right) = 12 \times \frac{1}{3}\).
The first term is \(4\).

As printed the data are inconsistent: with \(a = 16\) and \(S = \frac{96}{17}\), \(1 - r = \frac{a}{S} = 16 \times \frac{17}{96} = \frac{17}{6}\), giving \(r = -\frac{11}{6}\). But \(|r| = \frac{11}{6} > 1\), so that G.P. has NO sum to infinity — the stem contradicts itself. The intended sum is \(\frac{96}{7}\).
With \(a = 16\) and \(S = \frac{96}{7}\): \(1 - r = \frac{a}{S} = 16 \times \frac{7}{96} = \frac{7}{6}\).
\(\therefore r = 1 - \frac{7}{6}\), and \(|r| = \frac{1}{6} < 1\), so the sum to infinity does exist.
The common ratio is \(r = -\frac{1}{6}\).
_note: Book defect (adjudicated). The printed sum 96/17 forces r = -11/6, so |r| > 1 and the sum to infinity the question presupposes cannot exist. The printed key repeats this and gives -11/6, i.e. the key is consistent with the defective stem rather than correct. Solved against the intended 96/7, which gives the clean r = -1/6.

solution:
Let the G.P. be \(a, ar, ar^{2}, \ldots\) with \(|r| < 1\).
Sum of terms: \(\frac{a}{1 - r} = 5\), so \(a = 5(1 - r)\).
The squares \(a^{2}, a^{2}r^{2}, a^{2}r^{4}, \ldots\) form a G.P. with ratio \(r^{2}\), so \(\frac{a^{2}}{1 - r^{2}} = 15\).
Substituting: \(\frac{25(1 - r)^{2}}{(1 - r)(1 + r)} = 15 \Rightarrow \frac{25(1 - r)}{1 + r} = 15 \Rightarrow 25 - 25r = 15 + 15r \Rightarrow 40r = 10\), so \(r = \frac{1}{4}\) and \(a = 5\left(\frac{3}{4}\right) = \frac{15}{4}\).
The G.P. is \(\frac{15}{4}, \frac{15}{16}, \frac{15}{64}, \ldots\)

The summation starts at \(r = 1\), so the terms are \(4(0.5), 4(0.5)^{2}, 4(0.5)^{3}, \ldots\) — a G.P. with first term \(a = 4(0.5) = 2\) and ratio \(0.5\), and \(|0.5| < 1\).
\(\sum_{r=1}^{\infty} 4(0.5)^{r} = \frac{2}{1 - 0.5} = \frac{2}{0.5}\).
The sum is \(4\).

The summation starts at \(r = 1\), so the first term is \(a = -\frac{1}{3}\) and the common ratio is \(-\frac{1}{3}\), with \(\left|-\frac{1}{3}\right| < 1\).
\(\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)^{r} = \frac{-\frac{1}{3}}{1 - \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)} = \frac{-\frac{1}{3}}{\frac{4}{3}}\).
The sum is \(-\frac{1}{4}\).

Here the summation starts at \(r = 0\), so the first term is the \(r = 0\) term \((-8)\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{0} = -8\), and the common ratio is \(-\frac{1}{2}\), with \(\left|-\frac{1}{2}\right| < 1\).
\(\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}(-8)\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{r} = \frac{-8}{1 - \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)} = \frac{-8}{\frac{3}{2}} = -8 \times \frac{2}{3}\).
The sum is \(-\frac{16}{3}\).
_note: Disagrees with the printed key, which gives 8/3. That value is the sum from r = 1 onwards; this summation is printed with lower limit r = 0 (verified at high zoom and adjudicated), and the extra r = 0 term is -8, so -8 + 8/3 = -16/3. Our answer follows the printed lower limit.

solution:
The summation starts at \(n = 1\), so the first term is \(a = 0.4\) and the common ratio is \(0.4\), with \(|0.4| < 1\).
\(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 0.4^{n} = \frac{0.4}{1 - 0.4} = \frac{0.4}{0.6}\).
The sum is \(\frac{2}{3}\).

Joining the midpoints of a square of side \(s\) gives a square whose side is half the diagonal of the original, i.e. \(\frac{s}{\sqrt{2}}\); so each new area is half the previous area.
The areas are \(1, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}, \ldots\) — an infinite G.P. with \(a = 1\), \(r = \frac{1}{2}\), \(|r| < 1\).
\(S = \frac{1}{1 - \frac{1}{2}}\).
The sum of the areas of all the squares is \(2\) square units.

Each new square has side \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) times the previous side, so each perimeter is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) times the previous one.
The perimeters are \(4, \frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{4}{2}, \ldots\) — an infinite G.P. with \(a = 4\), \(r = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), \(|r| < 1\).
\(S = \frac{4}{1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}} = \frac{4\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2} - 1} = \frac{4\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2} + 1)}{(\sqrt{2} - 1)(\sqrt{2} + 1)} = 4(2 + \sqrt{2})\).
The sum of the perimeters of all the squares is \(\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2} - 1} = 8 + 4\sqrt{2}\) units.

Each rebound reaches \(\frac{6}{10} = 0.6\) of the previous height (check: \(\frac{3.6}{6} = 0.6\)).
The ball first falls \(10\) m; thereafter it rises to each of \(6, 3.6, 2.16, \ldots\) m and falls through the same height again, so every rebound height is travelled twice.
Total distance \(= 10 + 2(6 + 3.6 + 2.16 + \cdots) = 10 + 2 \times \frac{6}{1 - 0.6} = 10 + 2 \times 15\).
The total distance travelled by the ball is \(40\) m.
_note: Disagrees with the printed key, which gives 25 m. 25 = 10 + 6/(1 - 0.6) counts each rebound height only once, i.e. it counts the ball going up but not coming back down. Since the ball returns to the ground after every bounce, each rebound height is travelled twice, giving 10 + 2(15) = 40 m.

solution:
A sequence is an H.P. when the sequence of reciprocals is an A.P.
Reciprocals: \(3, 5, 7, 9, \ldots\), with differences \(5 - 3 = 7 - 5 = 9 - 7 = 2\), a constant.
The reciprocals form an A.P. with \(d = 2\), so the given sequence is an H.P.

Reciprocals: \(3, 6, 12, 24, \ldots\), with differences \(6 - 3 = 3\) but \(12 - 6 = 6\).
The differences are not constant, so the reciprocals are not an A.P. (they form a G.P. with ratio \(2\)).
The given sequence is not an H.P.

Reciprocals: \(\frac{1}{5}, \frac{17}{10}, \frac{32}{10}, \frac{47}{10}\), i.e. \(\frac{2}{10}, \frac{17}{10}, \frac{32}{10}, \frac{47}{10}\).
Differences: \(\frac{15}{10} = \frac{3}{2}\) each time.
The reciprocals form an A.P. with \(d = \frac{3}{2}\), so the given sequence is an H.P.

Reciprocals: \(2, 5, 8, 11, \ldots\) — an A.P. with \(a = 2\), \(d = 3\).
Its \(n^{\text{th}}\) term is \(a + (n - 1)d = 2 + (n - 1)3 = 3n - 1\).
\(\therefore\) the \(n^{\text{th}}\) term of the H.P. is \(t_{n} = \frac{1}{3n - 1}\), and \(t_{8} = \frac{1}{3(8) - 1} = \frac{1}{23}\).
\(t_{n} = \frac{1}{3n - 1}\) and \(t_{8} = \frac{1}{23}\).

Reciprocals: \(4, 6, 8, 10, \ldots\) — an A.P. with \(a = 4\), \(d = 2\).
Its \(n^{\text{th}}\) term is \(4 + (n - 1)2 = 2n + 2\).
\(\therefore\) the \(n^{\text{th}}\) term of the H.P. is \(t_{n} = \frac{1}{2n + 2}\), and \(t_{8} = \frac{1}{2(8) + 2} = \frac{1}{18}\).
\(t_{n} = \frac{1}{2n + 2}\) and \(t_{8} = \frac{1}{18}\).

Reciprocals: \(5, 10, 15, 20, \ldots\) — an A.P. with \(a = 5\), \(d = 5\).
Its \(n^{\text{th}}\) term is \(5 + (n - 1)5 = 5n\).
\(\therefore\) the \(n^{\text{th}}\) term of the H.P. is \(t_{n} = \frac{1}{5n}\), and \(t_{8} = \frac{1}{5(8)} = \frac{1}{40}\).
\(t_{n} = \frac{1}{5n}\) and \(t_{8} = \frac{1}{40}\).

For two positive numbers, \(G^{2} = A \times H\).
Given \(G = 4\) and \(H = \frac{16}{5}\): \(4^{2} = A \times \frac{16}{5}\), so \(16 = \frac{16A}{5}\).
\(\therefore A = 5\).
The A.M. is \(5\).

For two positive numbers, \(G^{2} = A \times H\).
Given \(A = \frac{15}{2}\) and \(G = 6\): \(6^{2} = \frac{15}{2} \times H\), so \(36 = \frac{15H}{2}\).
\(\therefore H = \frac{72}{15} = \frac{24}{5}\).
The H.M. is \(\frac{24}{5}\).

For two positive numbers, \(G^{2} = A \times H\).
Given \(A = 75\) and \(H = 48\): \(G^{2} = 75 \times 48 = 3600\).
\(\therefore G = \sqrt{3600} = 60\) (positive, since the numbers are positive).
The G.M. is \(60\).

Let the required H.P. be \(\frac{1}{4}, H_{1}, H_{2}, \frac{1}{3}\). Then the reciprocals \(4, \frac{1}{H_{1}}, \frac{1}{H_{2}}, 3\) must form an A.P. with \(a = 4\) and \(t_{4} = 3\).
\(a + 3d = 3 \Rightarrow 4 + 3d = 3 \Rightarrow d = -\frac{1}{3}\).
So the A.P. is \(4, \frac{11}{3}, \frac{10}{3}, 3\), and taking reciprocals of the two middle terms gives \(\frac{3}{11}\) and \(\frac{3}{10}\).
The two numbers are \(\frac{3}{11}\) and \(\frac{3}{10}\).

Let the numbers be \(a\) and \(b\), with means \(A\), \(G\), \(H\). Given \(A - G = 2\) and \(A - H = \frac{18}{5}\), so \(G = A - 2\) and \(H = A - \frac{18}{5}\).
Using \(G^{2} = A \times H\): \((A - 2)^{2} = A\left(A - \frac{18}{5}\right) \Rightarrow A^{2} - 4A + 4 = A^{2} - \frac{18A}{5} \Rightarrow 4 = 4A - \frac{18A}{5} = \frac{2A}{5}\), so \(A = 10\) and \(G = 8\).
Then \(a + b = 2A = 20\) and \(ab = G^{2} = 64\), so \(a, b\) are the roots of \(x^{2} - 20x + 64 = 0\), i.e. \((x - 4)(x - 16) = 0\).
The numbers are \(4\) and \(16\).
_note: This question is word-for-word the same problem as the chapter's own solved example 2.6.3 SolvedEx.5, which is printed with a full solution two pages earlier. The duplication is the book's; answered here on its own terms.

solution:
Let the numbers be \(a\) and \(b\). Given \(A - G = \frac{1}{2}\) and \(A - H = \frac{25}{26}\), so \(G = A - \frac{1}{2}\) and \(H = A - \frac{25}{26}\).
Using \(G^{2} = A \times H\): \(\left(A - \frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} = A\left(A - \frac{25}{26}\right) \Rightarrow A^{2} - A + \frac{1}{4} = A^{2} - \frac{25A}{26} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{4} = A - \frac{25A}{26} = \frac{A}{26}\), so \(A = \frac{13}{2}\) and \(G = 6\).
Then \(a + b = 2A = 13\) and \(ab = G^{2} = 36\), so \(a, b\) are the roots of \(x^{2} - 13x + 36 = 0\), i.e. \((x - 4)(x - 9) = 0\).
The numbers are \(4\) and \(9\).
